quiz.q: Why can't you use `Rc<RefCell<T>>` to share mutable state across threads?
options: `Rc` and `RefCell` are deprecated
`Rc`'s reference count isn't updated atomically, so the compiler marks it unsafe to send across threads
`RefCell` only works with numbers
They work fine, it's just slower than `Arc<Mutex<T>>`
quiz.explain: `Rc`'s internal counter can be corrupted if two threads bump it at once. The compiler catches this at compile time by not implementing `Send` for `Rc`.

options: Deep-copies the value inside the `Arc`
Bumps an atomic reference count and returns another pointer to the same value
Creates a brand-new independent `Mutex`
Moves the value to the cloning thread, invalidating the original
quiz.explain: `Arc` clones are cheap by design — they share the same underlying allocation and just increment a counter, not copy the data.

options: `&mut T` directly
`Result<MutexGuard<T>, PoisonError<...>>` — `Ok` holds a guard that derefs to `&mut T`
`bool` — whether the lock succeeded
Nothing; it just blocks and returns `()`
quiz.explain: `.lock()` blocks until available, then hands back a `Result` wrapping a `MutexGuard`. The `Err` case only occurs if the mutex was poisoned by a panic while locked.

quiz.q: When does a `MutexGuard` release its lock?
options: You must call `.unlock()` explicitly
Automatically, when the guard is dropped (goes out of scope)
Only when the program exits
As soon as you read the value once
quiz.explain: `MutexGuard` implements `Drop`, which releases the lock. There's no manual unlock call — scoping the guard tightly is how you control lock duration.

quiz.q: Five threads each need to increment one shared counter. What's the idiomatic pattern?
options: Pass a `&mut i32` to each thread
`Arc<Mutex<i32>>` — clone the `Arc` for each thread, `.lock()` before mutating
Give each thread its own separate counter and sum them with a channel
Wrap the counter in `Rc<Cell<i32>>`
quiz.explain: `Arc` provides thread-safe shared ownership; `Mutex` provides exclusive access. Together they're the standard way to mutate shared state safely across threads.

quiz.q: What causes the classic two-mutex deadlock?
options: Using `Arc` instead of `Rc`
Two threads locking the same two mutexes in different orders, so each ends up waiting on a lock the other holds
Forgetting to call `Arc::clone`
A `Mutex` that contains a `String` instead of a number
quiz.explain: If thread A locks mutex 1 then mutex 2, while thread B locks mutex 2 then mutex 1, an unlucky interleaving leaves each thread holding one lock and waiting forever for the other.

quiz.q: How do you avoid the two-mutex deadlock described above?
options: Never use more than one `Mutex` in a program
Always lock the mutexes in the same global order across every code path
Wrap every `Mutex` in an `Arc` twice
Call `.lock().unwrap()` instead of `.lock()`
quiz.explain: Deadlocks from lock ordering disappear if every thread acquires shared locks in a consistent order — then the circular-wait interleaving simply can't occur.

quiz.q: What does the compiler do if you try to share a plain (non-`Arc`, non-`Mutex`) mutable reference across threads?
options: Allows it, but warns you
Refuses to compile — the type isn't `Send`/`Sync` for that kind of sharing
Silently clones the value per thread
Automatically wraps it in a `Mutex` for you
quiz.explain: Rust's `Send`/`Sync` traits are checked at compile time. A bare shared mutable reference across threads fails to compile rather than risking a data race at runtime.

flashcards.front: Share ownership of a value across threads?
flashcards.back: `Arc<T>` — `Arc::clone(&x)` bumps an atomic refcount (cheap); the data itself is shared, not copied.

flashcards.front: Mutate shared data safely across threads?
flashcards.back: `Mutex<T>` — `.lock()` blocks until free, returns a `MutexGuard` that derefs to `&mut T`.
Automatically when it's dropped (goes out of scope) — no manual unlock call needed.

flashcards.front: Standard pattern for shared mutable state across threads?
flashcards.back: `Arc<Mutex<T>>` — `Arc` for shared ownership, `Mutex` for exclusive one-at-a-time access.
`Rc`'s refcount isn't atomic and isn't `Send` — the compiler refuses to let it cross a thread boundary. Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` instead.
Two threads locking the same two mutexes in different orders — each ends up holding one lock while waiting on the other, forever.

flashcards.front: How do you prevent lock-ordering deadlocks?
flashcards.back: Always acquire shared mutexes in the same global order, on every code path, everywhere in the program.
`Result<MutexGuard<T>, PoisonError<...>>` — `Err` only if another thread panicked while holding the lock (a 'poisoned' mutex).
